newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean police enter German enclave; raid possible.
newsitem.headline: Chilean police enter German enclave; raid possible.

text.p: About 30 police officers entered, then retreated to the edge of, a secretive German settlement in southern Chile on Tuesday, and a key official said a raid to arrest its fugitive leader could follow.

A convoy of police vans and trucks passed the first gate of Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) but stopped short of an inner gate leading into the shadowy community's living areas, where founder Paul Schaeffer, wanted on child abuse and other charges, may be holed up.

Under a steady drizzle, the contingent later turned back to park at the community's edge in an operation that police on the scene called a "visual inspection." A small group of officers was allowed past the inner gate and inspected some nearby buildings with guards' permission, a private television station reported.

"We have precise instructions from the special prosecutor in charge of this case to carry out a visual inspection. It is not a raid," police commander Julio Poo said at the scene. "We have come to gather information," he said.

Church bells rang out inside the colony, and residents lit a huge bonfire, apparently signalling their alarm at what looked like the long-awaited storming of the community, where a few hundred German-speaking residents live behind barbed-wire fences.
In Santiago, Interior Minister Carlos Figueroa said officials were not sure if Schaeffer was inside the colony but police had warrants to storm the place if given the order.

"The arrest order (for Schaeffer) calls for the possibility of proceeding to raiding the place and forcing open its locks in case that's necessary," Figueroa said. "The police are fully allowed to do that."

Schaeffer, a stout, balding German man believed to be in his 80s, who has been charged with molesting boys, has long been presumed to be inside the sprawling estate in the Andean foothills near the town of Parral, 200 miles (320 km) south of Santiago.

He issued a blistering statement last week saying he feared for his life if he surrendered and believed he could not get a fair trial in Chile. His team of lawyers quit after he issued the statement, saying they had tried to persuade him to surrender.

Two confidants, both German citizens, and two Chilean members of the settlement surrendered to police last week to face charges including the illegal detention of a child, obstruction of justice and the destruction of public property. All four were later released on bail.

Schaeffer set up the colony in the mid-1950s. It was protected by the former military regime of Gen. Augusto Pinochet, and human rights groups have charged that the military used it as a secret detention and torture centre.

A special prosecutor appointed by President Eduardo Frei's government issued an arrest warrant for Schaeffer late last year on charges that he molested at least five Chilean boys whose parents had sent them to a boarding school in the community.
The child abuse charges alienated the colony's one-time allies among conservative Chilean politicians and the Roman Catholic Church, who have urged Schaeffer to give himself up.

Adding to the tension, a Chilean cameraman for a German television crew was bashed on the head by one of the colony's security men on Sunday while he was filming the colony from a nearby hillside, and he suffered a mild concussion.
The attack was strongly condemned by local politicians and news media and the Chilean Foreign Press Association.
A few elderly German women residents said at the settlement's gates on Monday night tpolice were persecuting them and they had not seen Schaeffer in months.
"We came to Chile for peace, and we don't know why we are being subjected to this. It is so unfair," one woman said, speaking in German and looking distraught.
